response.final_text:
I've proposed closing alert A-261023-0004 as a false positive (CLOSE_FP), with confidence 0.75. It's filed as case C-A-261023-0004 and is waiting for a human decision.

**Three facts that drove it:**
1. **The buy order was actually trading before the sale.** The trader's single buy order of 19,570 was placed one tick better than the best bid. It filled 3,568 (18.2% of its size) before the trader's only sell. That is more than six times the 587 sold, which meets the firm's test for a genuine working order. So the first spoofing feature, an order not meant to execute, is absent.
2. **The sale and the later cut were ordinary order management.** After the 587 sale, the trader cut the rest of the buy order by 14,437 through a size reduction, not a cancel. Under the closure standard, that is not a benefit from the sale, even though the round trip made +3 ticks and the price moved 2 ticks his way.
3. **None of the other warning signs are there.** The cycle did not repeat in the session and he has no prior alerts in 90 days. There were no market events, no other traders cancelling in the same second, no risk-limit events, and all orders sat at a single price.

**What would change my mind:** evidence that the order's size, not its trading, is what moved the market. That would be a book reconstruction (which I didn't run) showing the large bid pushed the best prices up from 9995/9999 to 9998/10000 before the sale and they snapped back after the cut. A longer look showing this pattern repeating on other days would do it too. Either would point to escalation.

The order was about 8 times the average visible depth and 39 times his typical order size (19,570 against 500). Level 2 should note that, but under the procedures size alone doesn't make it spoofing.
